what: Alexandria Real Estate Equities is a REIT that builds and rents laboratory space. Its buildings are not ordinary offices: they have the ventilation, vibration control, power and waste handling that wet-lab research needs, clustered in a handful of science hubs such as Boston's Seaport and Cambridge, South San Francisco, San Diego and the Research Triangle.
customers: Biotech companies, large pharmaceutical firms, medical-device makers, universities and government research institutes. Tenants range from pre-revenue startups taking a single floor to multinationals leasing entire campuses.
money: Long leases on lab and lab-office buildings, usually with annual rent escalators and tenants paying operating costs.
Tenant reimbursements, management fees on joint ventures and gains or losses on property sales.
moat: Lab buildings are expensive and slow to build, and scientists do not move easily once equipment is installed, so leases are long and renewals common. Alexandria owns clusters rather than scattered buildings, which lets it move a growing tenant into a bigger space nearby instead of losing it.
risks: Too much lab space was built at once. Developers across the main science hubs delivered new buildings into a biotech funding slowdown, so vacancy rose and asking rents fell.
Revenue has turned down, from $3.1B in 2024 to $3.0B in 2025, and the trailing twelve months show a net loss of about $1.4B, driven by writedowns on buildings worth less than their carrying value.
Debt is about $12.8B against a market value of roughly $7.3B, so the equity is a thin slice of the whole. Refinancing at higher rates eats into cash available for dividends.
Tenant quality varies. Small biotechs that run out of funding stop paying rent, and the space they leave is costly to re-let.
The share price near $41.77 is far below where it traded a few years ago, a sign that the market doubts the stated book value of the portfolio.
opportunities: If biotech funding recovers, demand for lab space recovers with it, and Alexandria owns the best-located supply.
New lab construction has mostly stopped. Once the existing surplus is absorbed, there is little new supply behind it, which historically precedes a rent recovery.
Selling non-core buildings and joint-venture stakes can repay debt and narrow the gap between the share price and the value of the real estate.
The fourteen analysts covering the stock average a $48.50 target, about 16% above the current price.
watch: Whether leasing volume and occupancy stop falling. In a REIT, occupancy turns before earnings do, so a few quarters of stable or rising occupancy would matter more than any single quarter's reported profit, which impairments distort.
